hints: Look carefully at Fig. 4.1 for J and list all the functional groups present, noting both carbonyl groups and the hydroxy group.
Recall which reagent gives an orange precipitate with any aldehyde or ketone, and which reagent distinguishes aldehyde from ketone.
Think about what happens when the $\text{O-H}$ bond of an alcohol reacts with reactive sodium metal and what gas is released.
walkthrough:
Map the functional groups in J**
Look at J: it has $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO-}$ which is a ketone, $-\text{CHO}$ which is an aldehyde, and $-\text{OH}$ which is a tertiary alcohol on the same central carbon. So J will respond to carbonyl tests and to alcohol tests.

Test for any carbonyl with 2,4-DNPH**
Both aldehydes and ketones give a condensation reaction with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine. Since J contains two carbonyl groups, you definitely get a positive result, which is an orange or yellow or red precipitate.

Distinguish the aldehyde with Tollens**
Tollens reagent, $\text{[Ag(NH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}\text{]}^{+}$, is a mild oxidising agent. It oxidises aldehydes but not ketones or alcohols. J has an aldehyde group $-\text{CHO}$, so $\text{Ag}^{+}$ is reduced to $\text{Ag}$ metal, seen as a silver mirror or grey solid.

Test the alcohol with sodium**
The $\text{-OH}$ group reacts with $\text{Na}$ to release hydrogen gas: $2\text{ROH} + 2\text{Na} \rightarrow 2\text{RONa} + \text{H}_{2}$. You see this as effervescence, bubbling or fizzing. Remember to state the observation, not the gas name, for the mark.

Final answer: 2,4-DNPH: orange / yellow / red precipitate.
Tollens reagent: silver mirror / grey solid precipitate.
sodium metal: effervescence / fizzing / bubbling.

hints: Find the carbon in J bonded to four different groups and check why it is chiral.
Recall that the two optical isomers must be non-superimposable mirror images, drawn with solid wedge and dashed bonds swapped.
walkthrough:
Spot the chiral centre**
Focus on the central carbon of J. It is joined to four different groups: $\text{OH}$, $\text{CH}_{3}$, $\text{COCH}_{3}$ and $\text{CHO}$. Four different single bonds means it is chiral, so J exists as a pair of enantiomers.

Draw the pair as mirror images**
Draw the central C with $\text{OH}$ up and $\text{CH}_{3}$ on a solid wedge coming out. Put $\text{COCH}_{3}$ on the left and $\text{CHO}$ on the right with one as a dashed bond going back. For the second isomer, keep $\text{OH}$ and $\text{CH}_{3}$ in the same places but swap left and right, so $\text{CHO}$ is on the left and $\text{COCH}_{3}$ is on the right. The two structures must be mirror images across the dashed line.

Final answer: Chiral centre is $\text{C(OH)(CH}_{3}\text{)(COCH}_{3}\text{)(CHO)}$.
Draw two mirror images: central C with $\text{OH}$ on top, $\text{CH}_{3}$ wedged below, and $\text{COCH}_{3}$ and $\text{CHO}$ on left and right with one dashed, swapped left to right in the second isomer.

hints: Compare K ($\text{-COOH}$) with M ($\text{-COOCH}_{3}$) and identify what alkyl group has replaced the acidic H.
Recall the standard reagents and conditions for converting a carboxylic acid to an ester with an alcohol.
walkthrough:
Recognise esterification**
K has $\text{COOH}$ and M has $\text{COOCH}_{3}$. The $\text{-OH}$ of the acid has been replaced by $\text{-OCH}_{3}$. That is ester formation from a carboxylic acid plus an alcohol, so the alcohol L must supply the $\text{CH}_{3}$ group.

Name L and conditions**
L is therefore methanol, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{OH}$. Esterification needs an acid catalyst such as concentrated $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ and heating under reflux to drive the reversible reaction to completion and prevent loss of volatile alcohol.

Final answer: L = $\text{CH}_{3}\text{OH}$ / methanol.
conditions = acid catalyst, e.g. conc. $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ / $\text{H}^{+}$, heat under reflux.

hints: Remember that addition polymerisation opens the $\text{C=C}$ double bond in M to give a $\text{C-C}$ single bond backbone.
Think about how the two substituents $\text{COOCH}_{3}$ and $\text{CH}_{3}$ end up on the same carbon in the repeat unit, with $\text{CH}_{2}$ on the other carbon.
walkthrough:
Open the double bond**
M is $\text{CH}_{2}\text{=C(CH}_{3}\text{)(COOCH}_{3}\text{)}$. In addition polymerisation the pi bond breaks and each alkene carbon forms two new single bonds along the chain, giving a $\text{-C-C-}$ backbone.

Assemble the repeat unit**
Draw $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{-}$ on the left with two H atoms, joined to $\text{-C(CH}_{3}\text{)(COOCH}_{3}\text{)-}$ on the right. Show two dangling bonds extending left and right from the backbone carbons to indicate continuation of the chain. The ester group remains unchanged.

Final answer: Repeat unit: $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{-C(CH}_{3}\text{)(COOCH}_{3}\text{)-}$ with continuation bonds through the backbone carbons.
Left C has two H atoms, right C has $\text{CH}_{3}$ below and $\text{COOCH}_{3}$ above.

hints: Use Table 4.2 to find which bond is present in monomer M but is lost when the double bond opens to form Perspex.
walkthrough:
Link the spectrum to the bond lost**
M is an alkene, so Table 4.2 tells you it absorbs at $1500-1680 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ for $\text{C=C}$. When M polymerises, every $\text{C=C}$ becomes a $\text{C-C}$ single bond. Perspex therefore has no $\text{C=C}$ and that peak disappears, while $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{C-O}$ ester peaks remain.
Final answer: M shows absorption at $1500-1680 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ due to $\text{C=C}$; Perspex does not, as the $\text{C=C}$ bond is lost on polymerisation.

hints: Look at step 1 where propanone $\text{(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}\text{C=O}$ gains both $\text{OH}$ and $\text{CN}$ on the same carbon.
Recall the classic reagent for nucleophilic addition of $\text{CN}$ to a ketone.
Look at step 2 where $\text{-C}\equiv\text{N}$ becomes $\text{-COOH}$ while the tertiary alcohol is unchanged.
Recall what type of reaction converts a nitrile to a carboxylic acid in aqueous acid.
Look at step 3 where a tertiary alcohol loses $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ to form the $\text{C=C}$ in K, and link this to the given $\text{Al}_{2}\text{O}_{3}$ reagent.
walkthrough:
Step 1, build the cyanohydrin**
Propanone, $\text{(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}\text{C=O}$, becomes $\text{(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}\text{C(OH)CN}$. The $\text{C=O}$ has added $\text{HCN}$ across it. Use $\text{HCN}$ itself or $\text{KCN}$ followed by acid, or $\text{NaCN}$ plus $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$. This is nucleophilic addition of $\text{CN}^{-}$ to the carbonyl carbon.

Step 2, hydrolyse the nitrile**
The product now shows $\text{CN}$ changed to $\text{COOH}$ to give $\text{(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}\text{C(OH)COOH}$. Nitriles hydrolyse in hot aqueous acid, so use dilute $\text{H}^{+}$ or aqueous $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ with heat. At AS level this is called hydrolysis, also accepted as substitution of $\text{CN}$ by $\text{COOH}$.

Step 3, dehydrate to the alkene**
The hydroxy acid loses water from adjacent carbons to give $\text{CH}_{2}\text{=C(CH}_{3}\text{)COOH}$, which is K. $\text{Al}_{2}\text{O}_{3}$ is a dehydrating agent that removes $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$. This is elimination, specifically dehydration of an alcohol to form $\text{C=C}$.

Final answer: Step 1 reagent: $\text{HCN}$ / $\text{KCN}$ with $\text{H}^{+}$ or $\text{NaCN}$ with $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$; type: addition.
Step 2 reagent: dilute $\text{H}^{+}$ / aqueous $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$, heat; type: hydrolysis / substitution.
Step 3 type: elimination / dehydration ($\text{Al}_{2}\text{O}_{3}$ given).
